title: Iterator for Combination
statement:
Design a class `CombinationIterator` that hands out, one at a time and in dictionary order, every way of choosing `combinationLength` letters from a given string.

- `CombinationIterator(characters, combinationLength)` receives `characters`, a string of distinct lowercase letters already in alphabetical order, and the size `combinationLength` of each combination.
- `next()` returns the next combination not yet handed out. A combination is written with its letters in the order they appear in `characters`, and the combinations come out in lexicographic order, smallest first.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` when at least one combination has not been returned by `next()` yet, and `false` otherwise.

`next()` is only called while a combination remains.
constraints: characters consists of distinct lowercase English letters in sorted order
At most 10^4 calls in total are made to next and hasNext
Every call to next has a combination left to return
notes:
## Intuition

With at most 15 letters there are at most C(15, 7) = 6,435 combinations, so the iterator can simply build them all once and then hand them out from a list. Backtracking produces them already in lexicographic order: it fixes the smallest possible first letter, fills the rest in every possible way, and only then moves the first letter forward. Because `characters` is sorted, choosing letters by increasing index is the same as choosing them in dictionary order. (Checking all 2^n subsets for the right size and sorting them works too, but does more work and needs a sort.)

## Approach

1. In the constructor, keep `picked`, the letters chosen so far, and call `build(0)`.
2. `build(start)`: once `picked` holds `combinationLength` letters, join it into a string, append it to `combinations` and return.
3. Otherwise try each index `i` from `start` up to `lastStart`, the last index that still leaves enough letters to finish. Push `characters[i]`, recurse with `i + 1`, then pop it.
4. `next()` returns `combinations[position]` and moves `position` forward.
5. `hasNext()` checks whether `position` is still inside the list.

## Example 1, step by step

`characters = "abc"`, `combinationLength = 2`. `build(0)` picks `a`, then `build(1)` picks `b` (`"ab"`) and `c` (`"ac"`). Back at the top, `lastStart = 3 - 2 = 1`, so `b` is the last first letter: it pairs with `c` (`"bc"`). So `combinations = ["ab", "ac", "bc"]`. The calls return `"ab"`, `true`, `"ac"`, `true`, `"bc"`, and finally `false` because `position` has reached 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(C(n, k) · k) once in the constructor; O(1) per `next` and `hasNext`.
- Space: O(C(n, k) · k) for the stored strings.

## Pitfalls

- Each recursive call must start after the index just used (`i + 1`), or letters repeat and order breaks.
- Without the `lastStart` bound the search still works but wastes time on branches that cannot be finished.
- `hasNext()` must not move `position`; only `next()` consumes a combination.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `combinations` | every combination, in lexicographic order |
| `position` | index of the next combination to hand out |
| `picked` | letters chosen so far in the current branch |
| `start` | first index the next letter may come from |
| `lastStart` | last index that still leaves room to finish |
| `combination` | the string `next()` returns |
